about.title: Built for health stress and everyday calm
about.body: CalmIq helps individuals manage health-related stress: soothing check-ins, simple calm routines, and recovery-comfort ideas (rest, pacing, gentle self-massage or actuator-style comfort guidance). Chat is a companion, not a clinic — when hands-on care matters, Calm+ members can request a physiotherapist session.
about.disclaimer: CalmIq does not diagnose, treat, or replace professional medical advice. Seek urgent care for severe or sudden symptoms.

comfort.title: Recovery comfort
comfort.support: Educational wellness ideas for everyday tightness and stress-related comfort — not medical care. Prefer timed breath resets? Try Calm Routines.
comfort.doneBody: Take what felt useful. You can revisit anytime, chat for a check-in, or open Calm Routines for a short timed reset.
comfort.disclaimer: These guides share general wellness and comfort ideas only. They are not medical advice, diagnosis, treatment, or guidance about medical devices. Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, dizziness, or anything that feels wrong. Seek urgent care for severe or sudden symptoms. Physiotherapist sessions remain a Calm+ feature.

self-massage.title: Gentle self-massage
self-massage.intent: Soft comfort-pressure ideas for stress-related tightness in shoulders, neck, and hands.

s1.title: Settle and soften
s1.body: This is a wellness comfort idea, not a clinical massage. Sit or stand where you feel steady. Soften your jaw and breathe easily. You will try light pressure only — never force, never “work through” sharp pain.

s2.title: Shoulders
s2.body: Place a hand on the opposite upper shoulder. Use slow, light circles or brief holds where it feels tense from stress. Keep pressure comfortable — like easing fabric, not digging in. Switch sides if you like.

s3.title: Neck sides
s3.body: With fingertips, gently stroke or hold the soft area along the side of your neck (not the front throat). Move slowly. If anything feels sharp, stop and rest. This is comfort exploration, not injury rehab.

s4.title: Hands and wrists
s4.body: Massage the base of each thumb and the soft palm with easy pressure. Open and close the hand a few times. Useful after long typing days — still wellness only, not a promise of pain relief.

s5.title: Stop cues
s5.body: Stop immediately for sharp pain, tingling that worsens, swelling, or dizziness. Skip self-massage over bruises, open skin, or areas a clinician told you to rest. Comfort ideas are optional; resting is always allowed.

s6.title: Close gently
s6.body: Drop your shoulders once more and take a slower exhale. If tightness keeps returning or limits your day, consider Calm Routines for a short reset, chat for a check-in, or the escalate guide when human care may help.

comfort-tools.title: Comfort tools
comfort-tools.intent: Optional warmth, gentle pressure, or soft vibration-style comfort as wellness education — not product pitches.

s1.title: Tools as options
s1.body: Some people like warmth, gentle pressure, or soft vibration-style comfort for stress-related tightness. These are optional wellness ideas — not prescriptions, endorsements, or clinical equipment. Skip anything that feels unsafe for you.

s2.title: Warmth
s2.body: A warm (not hot) pack or wrap on shoulders or lower back for a short stretch can feel soothing. Keep heat mild, check skin often, and never sleep on high heat. Stop if skin gets too warm or irritated.

s3.title: Gentle pressure
s3.body: A soft cushion, rolled towel, or gentle pressure aid can give a comfort cue while you rest. Keep intensity light. This is about ease, not forcing tissue change or “fixing” an injury.

s4.title: Soft vibration-style comfort
s4.body: If you already own a gentle vibration or massage-style consumer tool, short, light use on large muscle areas may feel relaxing for some people. Follow the maker’s safety notes. CalmIq does not sell or recommend specific products.

s5.title: Safety rails
s5.body: Do not use heat, pressure, or vibration tools on broken skin, numb areas, or where a clinician advised caution. Skip products that claim to fix health conditions. Here they are comfort options only — not clinical equipment.

s6.title: Choose what helps
s6.body: Keep what felt pleasant; leave the rest. For timed breath resets, open Calm Routines. If DIY comfort is not enough, see the escalate guide for human care paths, including Calm+ physiotherapist sessions.

escalate.title: When to get help
escalate.intent: Clear rails from DIY comfort toward human care — Calm+ physio sessions vs urgent or GP cues.

s1.title: Comfort has limits
s1.body: Self-massage, rest, routines, and optional tools can support everyday stress comfort. They are not a substitute for professional care when symptoms are strong, lasting, or worrying. This guide helps you choose a next step — without labeling your symptoms.

s2.title: Signs DIY may not be enough
s2.body: Consider human help if tightness or discomfort keeps disrupting sleep or work, worsens over days, follows an injury you are unsure about, or comes with red-flag feelings (severe sudden pain, chest pressure, trouble breathing, weakness, confusion). Trust your judgment to seek care early.

s3.title: Calm+ physiotherapist sessions
s3.body: For hands-on wellbeing support when you want a human physiotherapist, Calm+ members can request Sessions inside CalmIq. Free plans keep chat, routines, and these comfort guides; physiotherapist sessions stay Calm+-only. If Sessions are locked, open Packages to learn about Calm+.

s4.title: Urgent care and your GP
s4.body: For severe, sudden, or emergency-feeling symptoms, contact local urgent or emergency services — do not wait on chat. For ongoing concerns that are not emergencies, your GP or another licensed clinician is the right path. CalmIq chat can help you plan questions; it cannot replace them.

s5.title: You can return anytime
s5.body: Use comfort guides and Calm Routines when they help. Chat when you want a soft check-in. Escalate to Sessions (Calm+) or outside clinical care when DIY is not enough. Taking that step is part of looking after yourself.

breathing.title: Breathing reset
breathing.intent: A longer-exhale pattern to ease stress in about two minutes.

s1.title: Settle in
s1.body: Sit or stand comfortably. Soften your jaw and drop your shoulders. You will breathe with a slightly longer exhale — a simple way to signal calm, not a medical exercise.

s2.title: Longer exhale
s2.body: Inhale gently for 4, hold for 2, exhale slowly for 6. Repeat for a few cycles. Keep the breath quiet and easy — no forcing.

s3.title: Notice
s3.body: Pause. Feel your feet or the chair. Notice any ease without judging what is still tense.

s4.title: Easy rhythm
s4.body: Inhale for 4, exhale for 6, a few more times. Let the out-breath be the longest part.

s5.title: Close
s5.body: Return to your natural breath. Carry one slower exhale into the next moment of your day.

desk-reset.title: Desk reset
desk-reset.intent: Stand, loosen shoulders, rest your eyes, and take a short walk cue.

s1.title: Step away briefly
s1.body: Save your work if you need to. This is a short comfort break for desk stress — not physio or medical advice.

s2.title: Stand
s2.body: Stand up if you can. Plant both feet. Uncross your legs and let your arms hang for a moment.

s3.title: Shoulders
s3.body: Gently roll your shoulders up, back, and down a few times. Keep the range small and comfortable.

s4.title: Eyes
s4.body: Look away from the screen toward something farther away. Blink slowly a few times, then soften your gaze.

s5.title: Short walk cue
s5.body: If you can, walk to another room or along a short path. Even a minute of movement helps reset desk tension.

s6.title: Return gently
s6.body: When you sit again, keep one easy shoulder drop and a slower breath. Come back anytime you feel wound up at the desk.

wind-down.title: Wind-down
wind-down.intent: An evening downshift with lights, breath, and parking the phone.

s1.title: Evening pause
s1.body: This is a gentle wind-down for the day — wellbeing comfort, not sleep medicine or clinical care.

s2.title: Softer light
s2.body: Dim bright screens or lamps if you can. Aim for calmer light so your body gets an “evening” cue.

s3.title: Slow breath
s3.body: Inhale for 4, hold for 4, exhale for 8. A few quiet cycles — longer out-breaths, no strain.

s4.title: Phone park
s4.body: Place your phone face down or out of arm’s reach for a few minutes. You can return to it after this routine.

s5.title: Stillness
s5.body: Sit or lie comfortably. Notice the room around you. Let thoughts pass without chasing them.

s6.title: One more soft breath
s6.body: Inhale for 4, exhale for 8, a few times. Keep it lazy and quiet.

s7.title: Rest cue
s7.body: End here. Keep the softer light and slower breath into whatever comes next — rest, reading, or sleep when you are ready.
